newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Bears still reign on Slovak bourse.
newsitem.headline: Bears still reign on Slovak bourse.

text.p: A wave of bearish sentiment that has plagued the Bratislava Stock Exchange since the summer should continue to push prices lower until year-end despite recent signs of a recovery.
Analysts said the BSE, which has fallen some 25 percent since in August, shows superficial signs of revival, but thin trading volumes may mask the market's true mood.
"At present, there is a clear bearish trend on the market and it is not likely to stop until the next year," Peter Krutil of Creditanstalt told Reuters.
Krutil said current traded volumes are very small and may disguise the market's real trend.
The 12-share SAX index closed at 165.52 points on Monday, down from its high for the year of of 226.34 on August 20, and near its all-time low of 147.10 at the end of 1995.
Many analysts said that while the bourse does not appear to be in danger of reaching a new all-time low, it could fall another 3-5 percent by the end of the year.

"The decline will continue at least until prices are more attractive. Then a war of nerves will begin with the question being who will start to offer their shares first," said Martin Barto of ING Barings.
Though the market's bottom may be difficult to predict, the reasons behind its fall are not.
A long standing lack of liquidity became acute after the summer when key shareholders began to show an unwillingness to put their shares on the market.

Key investors, mainly from abroad, became tired of being stone-walled by intransigent shareholders and tired of the wild price fluctuations that occurred in the few shares that eventually did make it to the bourse floor.
"Domestic conditions are the main cause of the fall, but also new investment oportunities in Bulgaria and Romania, have caught the interest of investors," Vladimir Kuklis of bank CSOB said.
Clouding the market's future development is also a controversial securities law amendment that could spell disaster for the BSE if adopted.
Slovak parliament recently approved the amendment, which would enable major shareholders to cancel, at will, the trading of a share on the bourse.

President Michal Kovac later refused to sign the law and returned it to parliament for revision, but the amendment is widely expected to be rubber-stamped by the ruling coalition majority later this week without major changes.
"The market is waiting for the final approval of the amendment, and in what shape it will be," Krutil said.
"Then we will see whether it (the amendment) will be recognised as a disaster, or not as bad as had been expected."
